subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a baby dragon scene sitting beside a broken speckled egg shell, aiming for a single reasonably complete three.js module of manageable length. I'm sketching proportions, roughly house-cat sized, around 0.25m tall sitting with a 0.45m body length, while being careful to keep all API usage correct since I can't test it directly.

I'm figuring out the egg shell as a lathe-based shape forming a bowl with a jagged broken edge, positioned beside the dragon, and setting up a simple skeleton with the hips as the root for a sitting pose. I'm also defining the color palette for the dragon's scales, belly, spine, horns, wings, eyes, and the egg's speckled texture, along with a few small smoke puffs for atmosphere.

Now I'm building the joint chain for the spine, neck, and head using Catmull-Rom paths — the hips serve as the root joint, the spine chain runs upward with three segments, and the neck chain branches off the top spine joint before connecting to the head joint.

Defining the jaw joint...

For the head shape itself, I'm considering a loft along stations defined relative to the head joint's local frame, with forward/up offsets controlling the profile width and height from brow to chin, attached to the head bone.

For the body, I'm planning a sweep along the spine chain with a radius function controlling girth, skinned to the hips/spine bones, with countershading between a teal back and cream belly based on surface orientation.

For back spikes, I'll place them using sweep.at(t) to get dorsal-facing frames so each spike stands upright from the body's outward normal rather than along the spine's tangent.

For the body sweep itself, I'm settling on using the spine chain as source with a bone list including hips plus spine joints, and working out a radius function that tapers to give a chubby hip-to-chest profile for a sitting pose.

Now I'm figuring out the tail: a small chain branching off the hips, curving backward and down to the ground using a catmull spline. I need to check the hips height against the body radius so the sitting rump actually touches the floor rather than floating, which means adjusting the hips y-coordinate accordingly.

I'm tapering the tail radius toward the tip and planning a spade-shaped cap extruded at the tail's endpoint, figuring out how to orient the extrusion plane relative to the tail direction.

Since the tail travels back in the Y-Z plane, I decide the spade should be drawn in that plane too, so it reads as a flat heart-like shape when viewed from the side. Working out the outline coordinates...

Still shaping the spade outline coordinates...

Computing the cross product confirms thickness runs along X, giving the broad side view I wanted. Now I'm figuring out where to anchor the spade at the tail's end point.

Now I'm working through the sitting pose for the legs, planning hip, knee, and ankle positions for the folded hind legs with the thighs angled forward.

For the feet, I'm figuring out how to render a flattened foot shape at the ankle and thinking through a simple way to add three small toes without overcomplicating the geometry, keeping things symmetric across left and right.

Still writing toe placement...

Now I'm moving on to the arms and oversized wings, planning shoulder joints and a wing root near the back of the spine with membranes stretched between finger-like bones — wings too large and clumsy for actual flight.

Building the wing membranes...

Setting up the wing chain parented to the spine with named shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, then building finger chains as short polylines from the wrist to each fingertip, naming each resulting joint.

For the wing membrane skin, I'm figuring out whether to pass full chains or raw point pairs between adjacent finger edges and the wrist, and deciding which joint to bind as the membrane's bone so it deforms correctly with the pose -- settling on using the wrist joint as the reference bone for the skin stretching between elbow and fingertips.

I'll use three membranes per wing side: one between finger1 and finger2, one between finger2 and finger3, and one connecting finger3 back to a body edge near the shoulder/hip, keeping all polyline edges running root-to-tip consistently. Now I'm defining the actual joint coordinates for each side using a sign convention where s=1 corresponds to the left side, starting with shoulder and elbow positions.

Still placing coordinates...

I'm also setting up small front arms with a three-joint chain from shoulder to hand, plus a tiny hand sphere and claw spikes, in addition to the wrist and fingertip positions for the wing membranes.

Now I'm working out the hind leg chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints, placing a flattened foot sphere at the ankle so it sits flush against the floor.

For toes, I'm looping over three positions to create small capsule claws anchored to the ankle bone, colored ivory. Then I'm starting to lay out the head and neck chain, sketching a path of joints running up from the spine through the neck to the head position.

I'm figuring out the head joint's placement and orientation so it aims forward-upward relative to the final neck joint, then defining the skull's loft stations with widths and heights to shape a compact cat-sized dragon head.

Finishing the snout stations, I move to the lower jaw: placing its joint beneath the head, aiming it forward and down, and lofting a tapering set of stations for the jaw shape with an ivory tint. Adding teeth as small spike shapes...

For the eyes, I'm positioning amber spheres on the sides of the skull using a surface-nearest-point approach, so the eyes sit embedded on the actual mesh surface rather than at a fixed offset. I'll add small dark slit pupils positioned similarly on that same surface hit.

Still working out eye and pupil placement...

Adjusting pupil placement...

Now I'm figuring out the horns on top of the skull, angling them backward using a direction vector and spike size, then thinking about adding spines down the back using repeated spikes along the body sweep.

For the tail, I decide to build a separate sweep so I can place dorsal spines along it too, rather than using the raw chain which faces the wrong way. I also pick a lighter amber tone for the wing membranes and sketch out nostril placement for a trailing smoke effect using a short series of small spheres.

Working out the smoke curl path...

I'll assume local(p) returns a Vector3 with .x accessible. For the smoke effect, I'll skip building individual puff spheres and just do a tail sweep, maybe adding a couple small grey sphere parts at points along the path to simulate puffs.

Now for the broken egg shell beside the dragon, I'm working out a lathe profile — a bowl-like shape with outer and inner curves forming the cracked opening, positioned at a slight offset from the dragon's body.

Still shaping the shell outline...

For texture, I'll apply speckled paint over the cream-colored shell base, scattering small brown spots to mimic natural eggshell patterning, with the rim left jagged by alternating sharp outline points.

Now I'm thinking through a couple of broken shell shards as thin extruded triangles placed near the egg, checking that the egg's position (offset to the left, radius about 0.085) leaves enough clearance from the dragon's body and hind leg so nothing overlaps.

For materials, I'm picking a teal base with a buttery belly tone, applying countershading to the body, and adding warm amber for the eyes and orange-gold for the translucent wing membrane. I'm also starting to work out the radius profile for the body sweep.

Checking the radius function...

Defining leg and arm chains...

To avoid naming conflicts I'll rename the wing joints to wingRoot, wingElbow, wingWrist, and keep arms as armUp, armFore, hand. For wing fingers I'm chaining a short polyline from wrist to tip per digit, parented to the wing tip.

Now I'm working out how membranes connect finger edges to the body, aligning each edge consistently from root to tip so finger3's wrist-to-tip pairs correctly with a body-side edge running from wrist toward the flank point.

I'm adjusting the flank anchor point so the membrane doesn't stretch through the body, settling on a position behind the spine. Now I'm planning the back spikes: seven orange spines running along the body sweep, each a small tapered cone.

For the tail, I'm designing a chubby tapering tail chain from hips backward using a catmull path, ending near the ground, then adding a spade-shaped tip in an amber color at its end.

For the body, I'm applying a countershade coat variable blending teal and belly colors, then using that on the head, jaw, and neck sweeps, with the neck tapering from a wider base near the spine up toward the head. For the limbs, I'm sweeping chubby arm chains with the coat color and adding spherical hands at the tips.

Now I'm positioning claws as small tapered spikes angled downward-forward from the hand tip, looping three across to form a set, then working out the leg chain points from hip to knee to ankle with a tapering thigh-to-shin radius and foot placement near the ankle tip.

For the foot I'm placing a flattened sphere at the ankle with scaling to make it wider and shorter, then adding three toe capsules fanning slightly outward from the foot, each tapering to a claw tip. Now I'm moving on to head details -- the skull and snout loft, then working out the jaw joint's position and orientation relative to the head so the jaw stations align correctly along its own local frame.

For the jaw loft I'm defining a few width/height stations positioned near the pivot point using head-local coordinates, tapering from wide at the back to narrow at the tip, and aiming the jaw bone forward and slightly down toward a target point. I'm also considering posing the jaw with a slight rotation to give the mouth a subtly open, grinning look.

For the lower teeth, I'm placing small upward-pointing spikes explicitly bound to the jaw bone so they move with it, since points built from head-local coordinates alone wouldn't inherit bone attachment correctly -- explicit bone binding takes priority and keeps everything rigged properly even after posing.

Actually, I'll skip the jaw pose rotation entirely to keep things simple and give a slight grin through the aim direction instead. For teeth placement, I'm laying out upper teeth as spikes along the front edge of the muzzle in a few columns, roughly 8 upper teeth plus 6 lower ones, positioned so they sit near the jaw's edge without overcomplicating the part count.

Now I'm working out stubby horn placement by finding the nearest point on the skull surface to seed them from.

Adding horn spikes...

For the eyes, I'm placing a large amber sphere near the top of the muzzle using the skull's nearest-surface point, mirrored left/right with a sign factor, then adding a smaller dark pupil sphere slightly offset and embedded into the eye socket.

I'm positioning the nostrils by finding the snout's front-top surface point and nudging the offset downward so they sit flush on the snout instead of floating above it.

For the smoke, I'm building a curved path rising from the nostril using plain coordinate arrays (avoiding Vector3 math), sweeping it with a radius that grows along the curl to mimic expanding smoke, and capping it with a couple of soft puff spheres near the top to suggest dissipating wisps, all colored a pale grey and attached to the head bone.

For the tail I'm adding a row of spikes spaced along the tail sweep using an "along" helper to place several spine shapes between set intervals. For the egg I'm defining a lathed shape with a jagged rim outline and a mottled paint pattern using base and spot colors, positioning it with an offset and axis, though I need to sort out the typing issue where mixing numeric coordinates with a "sharp" marker string in the outline array confuses the inferred type.

Still working out the egg's rim geometry...

Working through the rim geometry, I realize the jagged edge is really a zigzag in height at a narrow radius band rather than a radius change -- the outer wall rises to about 0.08-0.088, then the rim zigzags between radius 0.074-0.078 with heights bouncing from 0.12 to 0.145, before the inner wall drops back down at a slightly smaller radius, making sure none of these segments cross each other.

I'm reconsidering whether this should be a solid shape or a true hollow bowl -- a solid egg-half with a zigzag top would look fine from outside but wouldn't show an interior cavity from above, so I need an actual inner wall dropping to a floor to make the bowl's inside visible.

Still working out the shell coordinates...

Checking the other rim edges, they don't appear to cross the inner path either, and the x-coordinates stay non-negative throughout, so the outline should be safe from self-intersection. The speckled egg's broken zigzag rim looks right, though I'm wary that adding smoothing could round off sharp corners and risk crossing errors on these small features.

I'll go with smoothing 0 since the lathe points are already dense enough to give a nice egg curvature without it, and use 14 lathe segments for a reasonably smooth low-poly shape. For the shard, I'm laying out a simple triangle outline and extruding it with thickness along x, positioning it on the ground away from the egg and dragon's leg so it doesn't collide, with its bottom resting right at y=0 so it sits flush on the floor.

For color, I'm using a countershade paint that layers a scale pattern in teal tones over the back and fades to the buttery belly color underneath, applying COAT across the body, neck, tail, legs, and arms while reserving the belly tone for the jaw. I'm double-checking my import list too, making sure I'm not pulling in unused utilities like rng or limb that could trip up type-checking.

I'm now sketching the builder setup—importing createBuilder, countershade, scales, and spots from the agentic-3js-builder package along with the OutlinePoint type, then defining the model with createBuilder and exporting a meta object with name and description. I'm structuring the hips as the root joint with no parent, then chaining the spine off it, using a catmull spline path for the spine chain with named segments like spine1 through spine3, and I need to double check the sweep range options for the body geometry along that path.

Setting up color constants...

I'm defining the color palette and texture patterns, then building out the skeleton joints and spine/neck chains using catmull-rom curves, making sure the neck connects smoothly to where the spine leaves off.

Continuing the skeleton, I'm adding the head and jaw joints aimed relative to the neck, a tail chain curving backward from the hips with a spade-shaped tip, and now setting up the leg and arm joint chains symmetrically for left and right sides.

Writing wing and finger chains...

Adding leg sweeps, feet, and toe capsules...

Still building body shapes...

For the jaw loft and skull surface, I'm using the surface helper to get a queryable shape so I can place eyes by finding the nearest point on the skull relative to the head's local forward/side/up offsets, then sticking sphere geometry for the eyeball and a scaled smaller sphere for the pupil slightly offset upward.

For horns I'm computing a nearest point near the brow and calling a spike helper with a direction vector, length, and radius — but I realize the sign convention for "right" is inverted relative to world X, so the horn direction needs to flip sign to actually point outward rather than crossing inward; I need to fix that mismatch and double check the wing placement follows the same symmetry convention.

Now I'm placing the upper teeth as rows of small spikes along the snout, checking that their vertical position lines up with the actual bottom edge of the snout cross-sections at each forward station so the teeth sit flush rather than floating or clipping through.

I'm then adjusting the lower jaw teeth so their spacing matches the jaw's loft width at each forward position, narrowing the right-offset for the stations where the jaw is thinner near the tip, so the teeth stay within the jaw's silhouette while still forming a visible open-mouth grin.

Adding spine spikes along the body sweep...

Now I'm extruding the tail spade: anchoring it at the tail tip with an outward-facing orientation, defining a heart-like outline for the blade shape, and checking that the stem origin aligns correctly with the tail end point.

I'm also computing the thickness axis via the cross product of the x and y directions to confirm it runs correctly along the local X, and I'm picking an amber color for the spade with slight corner smoothing. Then I'm starting to sketch a smoke wisp as a catmull-rom path built from offsets relative to the head's local point, curving upward and outward in a few stepped segments.

Now I'm sweeping that smoke path with a radius that thins toward the end, attaching it to the head bone, and adding a small sphere as a puff at the tip. I'm building an egg shape via a lathe profile positioned to the side, plus a jagged shard piece extruded from a small triangular outline near the egg to suggest a broken fragment, and considering adding a second shell piece for visual balance.

Checking that the egg doesn't collide with the dragon's hind leg or tail based on their positions—the gaps look sufficient. But stepping back, I realize the overall proportions are off: at roughly 0.7 units tall this reads more like a large dragon than a cat-sized creature, since a sitting house cat is only about 0.3-0.35 tall. I should scale the whole figure down to match a more cat-like size.

Rather than reworking every single coordinate by hand, I'm considering applying a global scale factor around 0.65 to compress the design proportionally, though that means restructuring how the numbers are generated rather than hardcoding literals everywhere.

I'll settle on a scale constant of about 0.68 and a small helper to scale all skeleton points and radii consistently, so I can keep writing coordinates in "design units" and just wrap them with the scaling helper when it matters.

Scaling design coordinates...

Still placing head geometry...

Placing teeth positions...

Then I'm positioning the legs with hip, knee, and ankle joints, scaling leg radius along the taper, and shaping the foot as a flattened sphere with toe capsules extending forward.

Moving to the arms, I'm defining a three-point catmull chain from shoulder through elbow to hand, tapering the radius and adding a hand sphere with small claw capsules angled outward. Then I'm laying out the wing structure with root, elbow, wrist, and three fingertip points to form the wing membrane shape, plus adding spine, neck, and tail spikes with their own lengths and radii.

Now I'm scaling down the egg geometry by 0.7 and working out its outline points, checking that the zigzag rim segments and inner shell path don't intersect each other.

Once the shell outline is settled, I'm double-checking the API signatures I'll be using for loft, spike, capsule, membrane, lathe, extrude, and stick, plus the typing for chain tips and joint locals, before finalizing the build function export.
